title: Chapter 03: Java, IntelliJ IDEA & Maven
description: Master Java's JVM and bytecode portability, SDKMAN! version management, IntelliJ IDEA Git hygiene, Maven project structure and lifecycles, fat JAR packaging with Shade, picocli CLIs with subcommands, and JUnit 5 unit testing.

sections.title: 1. Java, the JVM & SDKMAN! Version Management
sections.description: Understand how Java achieves Write Once, Run Anywhere via bytecode and the JVM, manage LTS versions with SDKMAN!, and tune JVM memory.

blocks.title: Write Once, Run Anywhere: Bytecode, JVM, JRE & JDK
blocks.content:
Unlike C (which compiles to OS/CPU-specific native binaries), Java achieves **Write Once, Run Anywhere (WORA)** via two steps:
1. `javac` compiles `.java` source into platform-independent **bytecode** (`.class`).
2. The target OS's **JVM** executes that bytecode—the exact same `.class`/`.jar` runs unchanged on Linux, macOS, and Windows (as long as the JVM version is $\ge$ the compiled target).

### Nested Layers: JVM $\subset$ JRE $\subset$ JDK
| Layer | Contains | Who needs it? |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **JVM** (Java Virtual Machine) | Bytecode execution engine + Garbage Collector | Core runtime engine |
| **JRE** (Java Runtime Environment) | JVM + Java Standard Library | End-users who only **run** apps |
| **JDK** (Java Development Kit) | JRE + `javac` compiler, `jar`, debugger & dev tools | **Developers** who compile & build apps |

Open-source distributions like **Eclipse Temurin** ship a full JDK.

> [!WARNING]
> **Exam Traps:** Bytecode (`.class`) is *neither* human-readable source *nor* native CPU machine code. A JRE can run `java`, but has **no `javac`**—you need a **JDK** to compile.

blocks.title: Java Compilation & Cross-Platform Execution Pipeline
blocks.caption: javac compiles .java source into platform-independent bytecode (.class), which any compatible JVM can execute.

blocks.title: LTS Versions, SDKMAN!, JARs & Garbage Collection
blocks.content:
### LTS Releases & SDKMAN!
Java releases every 6 months, with a **Long Term Support (LTS)** release every **2 years** (e.g., Java 17, 21, **25**). **SDKMAN!** manages multiple JDKs side-by-side:
- `sdk list java` — list available/installed JDKs (e.g., `-tem` for Eclipse Temurin).
- `sdk install java 21.0.6-tem` — install a JDK alongside existing ones.
- `sdk use java 21.0.6-tem` — switch version for the **current terminal session only**.
- `sdk default java 25-tem` — set the **global default** for all new terminals.

### Compiling, Running & Executable JARs
```bash
javac HelloWorld.java   # compiles to HelloWorld.class
java HelloWorld         # runs main() on the JVM
java -Xmx1024M -Xms1024M -jar app.jar nogui
```
- A **JAR (Java ARchive)** is a ZIP containing `.class` bytecode, resources, and `META-INF/MANIFEST.MF` (which declares `Main-Class`).
- `-Xmx` = **maximum** heap size; `-Xms` = **initial** heap size.

### Automatic Garbage Collection (GC)
No manual `malloc()`/`free()`. An object becomes **eligible** for GC once it is unreachable (last reference leaves scope or is set to `null`); the **JVM** decides *when* to reclaim it.

sections.title: 2. IntelliJ IDEA & Git Hygiene
sections.description: Distinguish shared project configuration from machine-local IDE files so your repository stays clean across operating systems.

blocks.title: What Belongs in Git vs .gitignore?
blocks.content:
IntelliJ IDEA creates a `.idea/` directory per project. Split files into two rules:
- **Commit (shared project config):** code style, shared Run/Debug configs, VCS mappings.
- **Ignore in `.gitignore` (machine-local / generated):** `.idea/workspace.xml` (open tabs/layout), `.idea/shelf/`, `.idea/libraries/`, `*.iml`, `*.iws`, `*.ipr`, Maven's `target/`, and OS clutter (`.DS_Store`, `Thumbs.db`, `*~`).

> [!TIP]
> Delete IntelliJ's auto-generated `.idea/.gitignore` and keep one clean root `.gitignore`.

blocks.title: Clean Root .gitignore for Java + Maven + IntelliJ
blocks.code:
## IntelliJ IDEA
.idea/libraries/
.idea/shelf/
.idea/compiler.xml
.idea/jarRepositories.xml
.idea/modules.xml
.idea/workspace.xml
*.iws
*.iml
*.ipr

## Maven
target/

## Linux / macOS / Windows
*~
.DS_Store
Thumbs.db
[Dd]esktop.ini

annotations.note: workspace.xml stores personal window layout, open tabs, and local history—never commit it.
*.iml module files are regenerated from pom.xml by IntelliJ's Maven integration.
target/ holds compiled .class files, test reports, and packaged JARs—always generated, never committed.

sections.title: 3. Maven: Project Layout, POM & Dependencies
sections.description: Learn Maven's standard directory conventions, GAV coordinates in pom.xml, the difference between plugins and dependencies, and the Maven Wrapper.

blocks.title: Maven Dual Role, GAV Coordinates & Maven Wrapper
blocks.content:
**Apache Maven** is simultaneously:
1. A **dependency manager**: it downloads external libraries from **Maven Central** (`central.sonatype.com` / `mvnrepository.com`) into your local cache (`~/.m2`), including transitive dependencies.
2. A **build automation tool**: it compiles, tests, and packages your application identically on every machine.

### The `pom.xml` & GAV Coordinates
Every Maven project is centered around `pom.xml` (Project Object Model). Every artifact is uniquely identified by its **GAV coordinates**:
- `groupId`: organization/namespace (e.g., `ch.heigvd`).
- `artifactId`: project name (e.g., `java-intellij-idea-and-maven`).
- `version`: current version (e.g., `1.0-SNAPSHOT`).

Together, `artifactId` and `version` determine the output JAR filename: `target/java-intellij-idea-and-maven-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar`.

### Plugin vs. Dependency (Critical Distinction)
- A **dependency** (`<dependencies>`) is a library your Java code *imports and calls* at runtime (e.g., `picocli`). It ships with your application (unless scoped to `test`, like JUnit).
- A **plugin** (`<build><plugins>`) performs a *build task* (e.g., compiling, shading a JAR, formatting). It does **not** end up inside your JAR.

### The Maven Wrapper (`mvnw` / `mvnw.cmd`)
Running `mvn wrapper:wrapper` generates `mvnw` (Linux/macOS), `mvnw.cmd` (Windows), and `.mvn/wrapper/`. Commit these to Git! From then on, run `./mvnw` instead of `mvn` so every developer and CI server uses the **exact same pinned Maven version** without needing Maven pre-installed.

blocks.title: Standard Maven Project Directory Layout
blocks.caption: Maven enforces a convention-over-configuration layout so every Java developer immediately knows where code, resources, tests, and build outputs live.

sections.title: 4. Maven Lifecycles, Goals & Fat JAR Packaging
sections.description: Understand how Maven's phases and goals chain together, and why standalone CLIs require the Shade plugin instead of maven-jar-plugin.

blocks.title: Lifecycles, Phases & Goals
blocks.content:
Maven organizes builds into **three standard lifecycles**:
1. **`default`**: builds, tests, and packages the project.
2. **`clean`**: deletes the `target/` build directory.
3. **`site`**: generates project documentation.

Each lifecycle is an ordered sequence of **phases**, and each phase executes one or more plugin **goals**:

| Phase | Bound Goal (Default) | What it does |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `validate` | *(core)* | Checks that the project and `pom.xml` are valid and complete |
| `compile` | `compiler:compile` | Compiles `src/main/java` into `.class` files in `target/classes` |
| `test` | `surefire:test` | Compiles and runs JUnit tests in `src/test/java` |
| `package` | `jar:jar` *(or `shade:shade`)* | Packages compiled bytecode into a `.jar` in `target/` |
| `verify` | *(integration checks)* | Runs verification checks on integration tests |
| `install` | `install:install` | Copies the JAR into your local `~/.m2` repository |
| `deploy` | `deploy:deploy` | Publishes the JAR to a remote repository |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **The Golden Rule of Maven:** Running any phase automatically runs **all preceding phases** of that lifecycle in order. Running `./mvnw package` executes `validate` $\rightarrow$ `compile` $\rightarrow$ `test` $\rightarrow$ `package`. Chaining two lifecycles like `./mvnw clean package` deletes `target/` first, then runs the `default` lifecycle up to `package`.

You can also invoke a **goal directly** outside any lifecycle, such as `./mvnw dependency:tree`, `./mvnw dependency:go-offline`, or `mvn wrapper:wrapper`.

blocks.title: Maven Default & Clean Lifecycles
blocks.caption: Invoking a phase (like package) triggers every prior phase in the default lifecycle; clean belongs to its own separate lifecycle.

blocks.title: Why maven-jar-plugin Fails with Dependencies (and How Shade Fixes It)
blocks.content:
With external dependencies (e.g., `picocli`), a plain `maven-jar-plugin` JAR crashes at runtime:
```text
Exception in thread "main" java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: picocli/CommandLine
```
- **Why:** `maven-jar-plugin` packages **only your own `.class` files**, omitting dependencies (even `<addClasspath>true</addClasspath>` only writes `Class-Path:` in `MANIFEST.MF`, requiring separate JARs alongside yours).
- **Fix (`maven-shade-plugin`):** During `package`, `shade:shade` unpacks and bundles all runtime dependencies into one self-contained **fat JAR (uber JAR)** with `Main-Class` in `MANIFEST.MF` (also emitting `original-*.jar` and `dependency-reduced-pom.xml` in `target/`).
- **Formatting:** `spotless-maven-plugin` enables `./mvnw spotless:check` and `./mvnw spotless:apply`.

sections.title: 5. Building CLIs with picocli & Testing with JUnit 5
sections.description: Design structured command-line interfaces with picocli options, parameters, and subcommands, and verify your logic with JUnit 5 unit tests.

blocks.title: Declarative CLIs with picocli
blocks.content:
**picocli** lets you build rich CLI tools (like `git` or `docker`) using Java annotations instead of brittle `args[0]` `if/else` chains:

- `@CommandLine.Command`: marks a class as a command or subcommand (`name`, `description`, `version`, `mixinStandardHelpOptions = true` for `--help`/`--version`, `subcommands = { ... }`, `scope = ScopeType.INHERIT`).
- `@CommandLine.Parameters(index = "0", defaultValue = "World")`: binds a **positional** argument.
- `@CommandLine.Option(names = {"-g", "--greetings"}, defaultValue = "Hello")`: binds a **named flag/option**.
- `@CommandLine.ParentCommand`: injects the parent command instance into a subcommand so it can read inherited parameters/options (e.g., `parent.getName()`).
- `implements Callable<Integer>`: `call()` executes the command and returns an integer exit code (`0` for success), which `System.exit(exitCode)` passes back to the OS shell.

annotations.note: Registers Hello and Goodbye as subcommands (invoked like `java -jar app.jar Alice hello`).
ScopeType.INHERIT shares Main's parameters/options with its subcommands.
Positional parameter at index 0, defaulting to "World" if omitted.
Executes picocli parsing, invokes the matched subcommand's call(), and returns its exit code.

blocks.title: Unit Testing with JUnit 5
blocks.content:
A **unit test** verifies a small, isolated piece of logic: given input $X$, function $f$ must return output $Y$.

In Maven:
- Tests live in `src/test/java/` and mirror the package structure of `src/main/java/` (e.g., `ch.heigvd.GreetingTest`).
- JUnit 5 (`org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter`) is declared with `<scope>test</scope>` so it is **never bundled** into your production JAR.
- Running `./mvnw test` (or `./mvnw package`) runs all `@Test` methods via `surefire:test`. If **any assertion fails**, the build **aborts immediately** before a broken JAR can be packaged.

> [!TIP]
> **Design for Testability:** Keep CLI I/O (`picocli` + `System.out.println`) thin and extract pure logic into testable methods like `Greeting.greet(String greetings, String name)`.

sections.title: 6. Synthesis & Metacognitive Calibration
sections.description: Diagnose real-world Maven packaging failures and dependency scoping.

blocks.title: Calibration: Diagnosing NoClassDefFoundError & Test Scope
blocks.prompt: A teammate's CLI runs fine inside IntelliJ IDEA, but fails with `NoClassDefFoundError: picocli/CommandLine` when they run `java -jar target/app.jar`. Meanwhile, they worry that adding JUnit 5 will bloat the final JAR. Explain both issues clearly.
self_check_criteria: Explained that IntelliJ puts Maven dependencies on the runtime classpath automatically, whereas `maven-jar-plugin` omits them from the packaged JAR.
Identified `maven-shade-plugin` as the solution to bundle runtime dependencies into a fat JAR with `Main-Class` in `MANIFEST.MF`.
Explained that `<scope>test</scope>` keeps JUnit 5 out of the packaged JAR while still running it during `./mvnw test` and `./mvnw package`.
blocks.model_answer: IntelliJ automatically passes all Maven dependencies on the `-cp` classpath when clicking Play, hiding packaging issues. When building with `maven-jar-plugin`, only the project's own compiled `.class` files are placed in the JAR, so `java -jar` cannot find `picocli/CommandLine` and throws `NoClassDefFoundError`. Switching to `maven-shade-plugin` unpacks and bundles runtime dependencies into a self-contained fat JAR. Finally, JUnit 5 is declared with `<scope>test</scope>`, meaning Maven uses it during the `test` phase (before `package`) and automatically excludes it from the final JAR.

sections.title: 7. Diagnostic Quiz & Spaced Repetition
sections.description: Test your understanding of Java, SDKMAN!, IntelliJ Git hygiene, Maven lifecycles, Shade, picocli, and JUnit 5, and consolidate key concepts with flashcards.

blocks.question: Which statement accurately describes the relationship between the **JVM**, **JRE**, and **JDK**?
options: They are nested layers: JDK contains JRE (standard library + JVM), and JRE contains the JVM.
They are three mutually exclusive installers depending on whether you use Linux, macOS, or Windows.
The JRE includes `javac` for compiling, while the JDK only executes pre-compiled JARs.
The JVM compiles `.java` files directly to native machine code ahead of time without bytecode.
blocks.correct_answer: They are nested layers: JDK contains JRE (standard library + JVM), and JRE contains the JVM.
blocks.explanation:
JVM, JRE, and JDK are nested layers: the JVM executes bytecode; the JRE adds the standard library so you can run programs; and the JDK adds `javac` and developer tools so you can compile and package programs.

* They are not OS-specific alternatives.
* The JRE does *not* include `javac`—the JDK does.
* `javac` compiles `.java` to platform-independent bytecode, not native machine code.
hints: Think of Russian nesting dolls: which one do developers install vs end-users?
Remember what the 'D' in JDK and 'R' in JRE stand for.

blocks.question: You have Java 25 set as your default, and you run `sdk use java 21.0.6-tem` in Terminal A. You then open a brand-new Terminal B and run `java --version`. What does Terminal B report?
options: Java 25, because `sdk use` only changes the version for the current terminal session.
Java 21, because `sdk use` updates the global default for all terminals.
An error, because two JDK versions cannot be installed simultaneously.
Java 21, unless you also run `sdk uninstall java 25-tem`.
blocks.correct_answer: Java 25, because `sdk use` only changes the version for the current terminal session.
blocks.explanation:
In SDKMAN!, `sdk use java <version>` modifies `PATH`/`JAVA_HOME` only in the **current shell session**. To change the default across all new terminals, you must use `sdk default java <version>`.

* SDKMAN! is specifically designed to keep multiple JDKs installed side-by-side.
hints: Does `sdk use` persist across new terminal windows?

blocks.question: Which of the following files or directories should be **excluded from Git** (listed in `.gitignore`) in a Maven + IntelliJ IDEA project? (Select all that apply)
options: target/
.idea/workspace.xml
*.iml
pom.xml
mvnw and mvnw.cmd
blocks.explanation:
`target/` contains generated build artifacts, `.idea/workspace.xml` stores personal IDE window/tab state, and `*.iml` files are regenerated by IntelliJ from `pom.xml`—all three belong in `.gitignore`.

* `pom.xml` is the core build definition and MUST be committed.
* `mvnw` and `mvnw.cmd` (along with `.mvn/wrapper/`) MUST be committed so everyone builds with the pinned Maven version.
hints: Ask yourself: is this file generated/personal, or is it required for a teammate to build the project?
Remember that the Maven Wrapper (`mvnw`) exists specifically to be shared via Git.

blocks.question: In `pom.xml`, what is the fundamental difference between a `<dependency>` and a `<plugin>`?
options: A dependency is a library your code uses (and ships with your app unless test-scoped), whereas a plugin performs a build task and does not end up in your JAR.
A plugin is downloaded from Maven Central, whereas a dependency must be compiled manually with `javac`.
Dependencies only run during `./mvnw clean`, whereas plugins only run during `./mvnw test`.
There is no difference; `<plugin>` is just a legacy alias for `<dependency>`.
blocks.correct_answer: A dependency is a library your code uses (and ships with your app unless test-scoped), whereas a plugin performs a build task and does not end up in your JAR.
blocks.explanation:
Dependencies (like `picocli`) are libraries imported by your Java code. Plugins (like `maven-compiler-plugin` or `maven-shade-plugin`) execute build goals during Maven lifecycle phases and are never packaged into your application JAR.

* Both plugins and dependencies are downloaded from Maven Central into `~/.m2`.
hints: Think about `picocli` vs `maven-shade-plugin`: which one does your Java code `import`?
Does the compiler itself get shipped inside your final JAR?

blocks.question: When you execute `./mvnw package` on a Maven project that has a failing JUnit 5 test in `src/test/java`, what happens?
options: Maven runs `validate`, `compile`, and `test`; the failing test aborts the build before `package` can create a JAR.
Maven skips `test` and packages the JAR anyway, printing a warning at the end.
Maven deletes `target/` first because `package` always implies `clean`.
Maven packages the JAR first, and only runs `test` afterward.
blocks.correct_answer: Maven runs `validate`, `compile`, and `test`; the failing test aborts the build before `package` can create a JAR.
blocks.explanation:
By Maven's lifecycle rule, running `package` executes all prior phases in order: `validate` -> `compile` -> `test` -> `package`. Because `test` runs *before* `package`, a failing unit test stops the build before any broken JAR is produced.

* `clean` is a separate lifecycle and is NOT run unless you explicitly type `./mvnw clean package`.
hints: Recall the order of phases in the `default` lifecycle: where does `test` sit relative to `package`?

blocks.question: Why did running `java -jar target/java-intellij-idea-and-maven-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar` throw `NoClassDefFoundError: picocli/CommandLine` before adding `maven-shade-plugin`?
options: `maven-jar-plugin` only packages your own compiled classes and does not bundle external dependencies into the JAR.
`picocli` had `<scope>test</scope>` in `pom.xml`.
The JVM cannot execute JAR files that contain more than one Java package.
`mvn wrapper:wrapper` was not run before `package`.
blocks.correct_answer: `maven-jar-plugin` only packages your own compiled classes and does not bundle external dependencies into the JAR.
blocks.explanation:
`maven-jar-plugin` creates a standard thin JAR containing only your compiled classes from `target/classes`. External dependencies like `picocli` remain in `~/.m2` unless you use `maven-shade-plugin` to bundle them into a fat/uber JAR.

* `picocli` has default `compile` scope (not `test`), yet `maven-jar-plugin` still does not embed it.
hints: What does `maven-jar-plugin` put inside the JAR by default?
Why do we call the output of `maven-shade-plugin` a 'fat JAR'?

blocks.question:
Suppose a picocli `Main` command has positional parameter `name` (`defaultValue = "World"`, `scope = ScopeType.INHERIT`), and its `hello` subcommand has option `-g`/`--greetings` (`defaultValue = "Hello"`) and prints `greetings + " " + parent.getName() + "!"`. What does running the following command print?

```bash
java -jar app.jar "Alice" hello -g "Salut"
```
options: Salut Alice!
Hello Alice!
Salut World!
Hello World!
blocks.explanation: The positional parameter `"Alice"` binds to `Main.name` (overriding `"World"`). Because `Main` uses `scope = ScopeType.INHERIT`, the `hello` subcommand reads `parent.getName()` (`"Alice"`) via `@ParentCommand`. The `-g "Salut"` option overrides `Hello.greetings` (default `"Hello"`), producing `Salut Alice!`.
hints: Trace which argument binds to `Main` (index 0) and which binds to `Hello` (`-g`).

blocks.title: Java Garbage Collection
blocks.front: When does an object become **eligible** for Garbage Collection in Java, and who decides when it is freed?
blocks.back: An object becomes eligible when it is **no longer reachable** (its last reference leaves scope or is set to `null`). The **JVM** decides the exact moment to reclaim it.

blocks.title: Maven GAV Coordinates
blocks.front: What are the three **GAV coordinates** in `pom.xml`, and which two determine the output JAR filename?
blocks.hint: G = group, A = artifact, V = version.

blocks.title: Maven Wrapper (mvnw)
blocks.front: What is the purpose of `./mvnw` / `mvnw.cmd` created by `mvn wrapper:wrapper`?
blocks.back: Committed to Git, the Maven Wrapper downloads and runs a **pinned version of Maven**, ensuring every developer and CI server builds identically without installing Maven manually.
blocks.hint: Pinned Maven version in the repo.
